[spoiler=Expansion Post and RP post][b]The Solar Covenant has been broken.[/b]

The throne of Shardju was the epicenter of the region since many generations. Its strength was as the sun on the flags. The Pharaoh was not just a king, he was also a living representation of order, equilibrium, and divine perpetuation. The temples affirmed him. He was backed up by the noble houses. The people survived under him.

Even a sun that hath never had his share Can seethe the land that he both should feed.

The Sun Throne was seized by Pharaoh Kharemun IV with tension. Breadth issues and magnanimous tensions heated under ritual harmony. Cautious consolidation had soon been transformed into iron rule.

Kharemun had concentrated power in an avaricious way. He terminated the provincial governors who were elected on the basis of good lineages and replaced them with those that were loyal to the palace. Audits and limitations of temple treasuries were instituted. The great houses were stripped of their ancient privileges in the charge of inefficiency and corruption. Grain levies rose. The army was restructured in a way that no house could have sufficient legions to present any threat.

Kharemun explained these reforms by the reason that it was needed to the immortality of Shardju. According to him, stability needed one will.

And Shardju had never been a single entity, but had been a balance.

The House of Menkara could boast the lineage to the first dynasties. The temple and throne had long been supported by their river estates on the central floodplain. The implication of an insult was clear when royal inspectors insisted on direct rule of Menkara irrigation on grounds of inefficiency.

Lord Tarek Menkara declined the decree.

His refusal was not shouted. He took a closed letter back to the capital, and with his unbroken sigill of the house.

Kharemuns reply was swift. He included a call-boy: Lord Tarek would appear in chains and answer the treason charges.

In its place the banners of Menkara fluted above their estates.

They made no proclamation of rebellion, they proclaimed restoration.

Weeks later, Houses of Sahuret and Khem-Dar became members of Menkara. Their declaration, dispatched via temple networks and provincial courts, charged Kharemun with the offense of breaking the Solar Covenant the ancient conception that the Pharaoh was not a solitary ruler, but a holy balance between himself and nobility and temple.

The declaration said, "Shardju is immortal. No one hand can boast to represent its entirety." It was rejected by the capital as Sedition. Arrests followed. Two smaller houses were disbanded. They had their patriarchs executed in the open as an example.

Western province Garrisons, who had been trained to be liaised to rebel houses, were reluctant when directed to march to confederate Menkara provinces. Some delayed. Others changed sides covertly. Cargos destined to be shipped to the capital were diverted. Citing the confusion of the bureaucracy, temple scribes diverted grain to the south to storehouses.

Civil war was not derived at one battle; it was as hairline fracture propagation among rock.

At the second year of violence, skirmishes erupted along the central floodplain. Loyalists occupied major crossings on rivers. Strongholds of estates were enforced by rebels. Both parties lacked overwhelming advantage so the focus shifted north.

Not far south of the Shardju frontier was Tareqet, a large basin of rich land irrigated by seasonal floods and complex irrigation. It had been a rich but disunited city-state system and coalition system decades old. Shardju was a trader with Tareqet, and also influenced it, but had never purported to be its owner.

Tareqet was not only a territory but also life to the rebel coalition. The rebels were in control of the bread, in case the capital was in charge of the treasury.

The northern campaign was headed by General Nefru Sahuret a silent strategist. His declarations talked of stabilization, safeguarding trade routes against banditry and providing the city-states of Tareqet with place in the irrigation systems, and defense assurances of Shardju.

Others capitulated quickly, because they feared being in the middle of fighting sides. Vassalies were entered into. Razing granaries were made. Shardju engineers built stronger levees and canals and posed themselves as allies.

The city-state of Qaret attempted to bring other lands together in a defensive alliance. Its militia had bravely battled beyond the walls, but could not compare with disciplined legions that had been in warfare. Qaret surrendered after being besieged. Its council was likewise placed under surveillance, and their fidelity insured by grain-contracts, and hostages of noble lineage paid with all ceremony.

The Tareqet basin was captured by the rebel alliance within one year under Shardju administration.

Where famine could have upset a divided kingdom, stocks were piled up. Markets stabilized. Soldiers were paid. The practice of offering sacrifices in temples in rebel-controverted areas reemerged with new confidence. During turmoil legitimacy succeeds bread.

Meanwhile, at the capital Kharemun increased his hold. He made the northern campaign illegal, executed by traitors. Loyalists attempted to break supply lines, however distance and increased opposition dimmed their effectiveness. Even cracks were seen in the palace bureaucracy. Scribes questioned edicts. Minor officials took a long time enforcing.

The Sun Throne, which nobody ever questioned, had been left alone with its golden walls.

The revolution became different in nature. It was no longer an apology in defence of aristocratic privilege. It turned into an alternative vision of the future of Shardju. The coalition stated that the Tareqet expansion guaranteed the prosperity of several generations, that the throne, house, and temple needed to be restored, and no Pharaoh could present himself as divinity and neglect the covenant.

Kharemun responded with proclamations of the God-send. He positioned the rebels as opportunists who were capitalizing on anarchy to undermine the sacred unity. Theatrical rituals became lavish, as it seemed spectacle would heal division.

On newly integrated lands that were in the north, the farmers were harvesting under the supervision of Shardju. A rebel protection saw merchants reopening trade routes. Soldiers in disputed provinces had dilemmas between allegiance and sustenance.

When the third year of war breaks, Shardju is a changed man. It has extended its borders northwards into some of the wealthiest agricultural areas in the area. It has never had more grain reserves. But there is a division in its heart. There are two authorities who purport to be the sun.

One is seated on the old throne in the capital, armed with tradition.

The other marches under banners of restoration, and is fortified by the breadbasket of Tareqet and the loyalty of the houses which know a different order.

The Covenant of the Sun is violated.
[/spoiler]

[b]January 1, 2028: Economic Report[/b]
The National Budget Committee has formally released a collation of the annual spending and earnings data for Rosenmarkke for fiscal year 2027.

The report notably showed increased growth in energy exports in Q4 of 2027 due to the formal opening of Rosenmarkket oil reserves to foreign markets, with energy exports making up 2.3% of trade outlays in 2027. 

Formal GDP growth showed an astonishing 5% year over year rise, with estimated 10% roll over growth expected by end of 2028. The GDP growth was primarily driven by increases in the services and manufacturing sectors under the National Readines Plan, however rains during the 2026 planting season bolstered the agricultural sector by 4.5% up 0.4% from 2026.

Trade was reported to have maintained steady, bringing in $789 Billion in exports, with a decrease in imports mainly impacted by Q2 and Q3 tariff hikes. 

Rates this year were cut from 5% to 3% leading to an increase in internal investments, though the stock market remains lower due to a drop in Q2. 

Preliminary budgeting plans show a 5% increase in welfare spending to 39% of the national budget, with armed forces spending being dropped to 5% along with a tightening of administrative costs with cuts to the budget there being expected by Q2 2028. (estimated to sit around 52-53% of GDP weight for 2028).

Inflation remained at a controlled 3.2-3.7% in 2027, though it remains above this committees target of 2.5%. It is estimated that initial integration costs for the 5th and 6th estates will lead to a spike in inflation in Q1 2028. 

This committee remains cautious about the state of the Rosenmarkket economy, and advises the government seek to loosen pressure on the economy with further trade and austerity measures.
